answers.java_tx_design: At Nordkontor, on our card-authorization service, I owned the transaction boundary around placing and releasing holds on a customer's available balance. Originally the hold placement and the downstream fraud-check call sat inside the same transaction, and under load the fraud service's occasional slow responses -- sometimes 2-3 seconds -- held row locks on the balance table long enough to cause contention during peak lunchtime traffic. I moved the fraud check outside the transaction, committing the hold first and running the fraud check asynchronously with a compensating reversal if it failed. The first version of that reversal had a bug -- if the reversal itself failed, a hold could stay stuck for up to 24 hours, which we only caught after a customer complained about an unavailable balance. We added a scheduled sweep job to catch stuck holds after that.
answers.java_ops: About a year ago our authorization service started getting OOMKilled on Kubernetes roughly three times a week, and p99 on the auth endpoint had crept up to 2.5 seconds during evening peak. I pulled GC logs and found we were running G1GC with a 3GB heap against a workload with heavy short-lived object churn from JSON serialization of authorization requests -- full GCs were happening every couple of minutes under load. I bumped the heap to 6GB and set MaxGCPauseMillis to 200ms, and separately found our connection pool was capped at 15 against a workload that needed closer to 40. After both changes, p99 dropped to under 400ms and the OOMKills stopped. I tried just scaling out to more pods first, which helped a little but didn't fix the underlying pause-time problem.
answers.rust_readiness: I haven't written Rust in production, so I want to be honest about that rather than pad it out. I've read enough to follow ownership and lifetimes at a conceptual level, and I understand async in Rust means choosing a runtime like tokio rather than getting one by default, the way Java gives you threads. If I were migrating something off Java, I'd want a narrow, well-defined boundary and real measurement before committing serious time to it -- though I'll admit that when I'm confident something is the right design, I don't always wait for that measurement to finish before I start building; I'd rather show people a working version and adjust from there.
answers.rust_boundary: If I were moving part of our ledger write path to Rust, I'd start with the settlement-batch calculation, since it's the most CPU-heavy piece and least coupled to real-time customer flows. Practically though -- and I know this isn't the popular answer -- when I've been confident a rewrite is the right call, I've sometimes just built the prototype myself over a weekend and brought a working version to review rather than spending weeks in boundary-design meetings first. It moves faster, and I've usually been right. I'd still want to measure hot paths before picking the exact boundary, but I wouldn't wait on a committee to tell me to start.
answers.money_correctness: At Nordkontor, our internal transfer service -- moving money between two customers' accounts, not external payments -- uses an idempotency key generated from the initiating request, stored with a unique constraint. About eight months ago, a client-side retry bug in our mobile app resent transfer requests without preserving that key correctly under poor network conditions, and over roughly six weeks we found 23 duplicate transfers that had slipped through, totaling around 2,150 euros in double-moved funds, none of it lost, just sitting in the wrong account temporarily. I found the pattern by querying for transfers with matching sender, receiver, and amount within a 60-second window, corrected each one with a new reversing transfer rather than editing the original records, and fixed the mobile client's key generation so it survived a retry. We also added a server-side dedupe check as a backstop, independent of the client behaving correctly.
answers.incident_response: The duplicate-transfer issue I just described is the incident I know best end to end. I noticed the pattern myself while looking at unrelated transfer-volume metrics -- nothing paged us, which in hindsight is itself a gap -- and told my team lead within the hour once I'd confirmed it wasn't a one-off. We had the mobile-client fix and the server-side dedupe backstop deployed within four days, and reconciled all 23 affected accounts within that same window. The postmortem's main change was that server-side dedupe backstop -- relying only on client-side idempotency had been the actual root cause -- and six months later, a similar client bug in a different flow was caught immediately by that same backstop before any duplicates went through.
answers.process_skipping: During the duplicate-transfer incident, I wanted to skip our usual second-reviewer requirement to ship the dedupe fix faster. I didn't -- I pulled in another engineer for a fifteen-minute focused review instead of our usual next-day cycle, which felt like the right middle ground, and they caught that my window check had an off-by-one on the boundary condition. Outside a live incident like that, I don't skip review or the deploy procedure; on a system moving customer money, I don't think saving twenty minutes is ever worth it when there's no real emergency forcing the call.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: A few months ago I pushed a schema migration that had a backward-compatibility issue with an older app version still in the wild -- nothing broke immediately, but I caught it in a log a day later and told my team lead and the mobile team the same afternoon, before it caused an actual incident. I've been on our on-call rotation for the payments team for about four years, roughly one week in five, and I still handle escalations from customer support when someone disputes a transfer. I've mentored two engineers through their first year, mostly around how to read our transaction logs. I don't think any of that is beneath what I should be doing -- it's usually how I find the bugs that matter.
answers.evidence_decision: A while back, the team decided, after a lot of discussion, to extend our existing rule-based fraud-scoring service rather than rewrite it as a new machine-learning-scored service I'd been advocating for. I disagreed -- I thought the rule-based approach had hit its ceiling -- but the team voted to extend it, citing the risk of a rewrite. I built the new scoring service anyway, on my own time over about three weekends, and brought a working prototype with real precision and recall numbers to the next planning meeting. It scored meaningfully better than the extended rule-based version, and the team ended up adopting it. I know that's not exactly 'following the decision' -- I'd do it again if I were that confident, though; showing people something working beats arguing in the abstract.
answers.own_contribution: In the fraud-scoring rewrite I mentioned, essentially all of it was mine -- I built the model, the scoring service, and the integration myself before bringing it to the team. The one part that was genuinely collaborative was the rollout plan afterward -- we agreed together on a staged rollout by transaction volume, 5% then 25% then 100% over three weeks, and that sequencing wasn't my call alone.
answers.java_recovery: A separate incident from the duplicate transfers: a batch job that recalculated daily interest accruals crashed partway through one night, leaving about 400 customer accounts with no accrual entry for that day out of roughly 60,000 processed. I found the gap by comparing the count of accrual entries written that night against our expected active-account count, wrote a backfill script that recalculated and inserted the missing entries using the same accrual formula as the original job, and verified it by re-running our nightly reconciliation against the interest-rate ledger the next morning, confirming all 400 accounts now matched. My first attempt at the backfill used the wrong day's interest rate for about a dozen of those accounts, since rates had changed at midnight; I caught that in the verification step and corrected it before it went further.
answers.java_perf_change: On the authorization service I mentioned, before the GC and pool fix, p99 was sitting at 2.5 seconds during evening peak; after, it was under 400ms, measured over a full week of peak traffic rather than a single good day. Before I found the GC issue, I tried adding a Redis cache in front of a lookup I assumed was the bottleneck -- that shaved maybe 50ms off the average case and did nothing for the tail latency, since the actual problem was GC pause time, not query cost. I left the cache in since it didn't hurt, but it wasn't the fix.
answers.rust_hands_on: I haven't written any Rust, production or personal. No point pretending otherwise.
answers.rust_when_not: I don't have Rust experience specifically. In general though, I'm skeptical of a blanket 'never rewrite' rule -- I think there are cases, like the fraud-scoring one I mentioned, where the existing thing genuinely can't be incrementally improved to where it needs to be, and building the better version and proving it beats months of committee debate. I'd probably apply that same instinct to a Rust rewrite if I ever became confident enough that a piece of Java code had hit its ceiling.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: Separate from the duplicate-transfer case, our monthly interchange-fee reconciliation was off by about 890 euros one month -- small relative to volume, but consistent, not random. I traced it to a batch of refunded transactions where the interchange fee had been refunded by the card network but our internal ledger still counted the original fee as owed, a timing mismatch between when the refund posted and when our reconciliation job ran. We corrected it with a new adjusting entry for each affected transaction, about 40 of them, rather than editing the original fee records, and moved the reconciliation job to run a day later in the month so refunds had time to settle first. My first theory was a currency-rounding issue, which I ruled out once the amounts didn't match a rounding pattern.
answers.prod_data_verification: I've been tempted to check something against live account data -- there was a point during the interchange-fee investigation where querying real balances directly would have been the fastest way to confirm my theory. I didn't; we have a daily-refreshed masked copy of the ledger with account-holder names and account numbers scrubbed but amounts and timestamps intact, and I ran my diagnostic queries against that. For something that genuinely can't be reproduced off production, our practice is a read-only shadow query, reviewed by a second engineer before it runs against anything live, and I've used that maybe three times in my time here.
